title: A Computational Framework for Evaluating Human-likeness in LLMs' Open-ended Human Behaviors
one_liner: Evaluate whether agent behavior matches human behavior by comparing large behavior patterns and by measuring rationality, consistency, and diversity across open-ended tasks.
lead: This paper addresses a basic evaluation problem for agent simulations: when a language-model agent shops, answers questions, or moves through a city, how should we judge whether its behavior looks human? One-off challenge prompts are weak because they depend too much on the challenge writer and do not scale across many settings. The paper instead compares model behavior with large collections of real human behavior data and scores three properties that matter in open-ended activity: whether actions make sense for the situation, whether choices stay coherent over time, and whether the population of behaviors is broad enough to resemble real human variation.

problem.h2: Why simple human judgments do not scale
paras: Many people judge human-likeness with a Turing-style test or a few hand-built scenarios. That approach can be biased because the chosen questions may favor some systems and miss important behaviors.

Open-ended human activity also has population structure. A believable agent should not only produce one plausible answer. It should produce patterns of action that resemble how many humans behave across many cases.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Replace one-off human judgment with population-level comparison between agent behavior and large real human behavior data.

panels.title: 1. Agents simulate people
panels.viz_args: Shopping choices, question answering, and mobility decisions
panels.caption: These agents are used in many studies, so their behavior quality matters.

panels.title: 2. Traditional testing is narrow
panels.viz_args: One interviewer asks a few crafted questions
panels.caption: A narrow test can be unfair because it reflects the examiner more than the full behavior space.

panels.title: 3. Collect real human behavior data
panels.viz_args: Large open-ended records from the web
panels.caption: Real data gives a target behavior pattern because it reflects how humans actually behave at scale.

panels.title: 4. Compare behavior patterns
panels.caption: The framework checks several principles because one metric alone cannot capture human-likeness.

panels.title: 5. Gap becomes visible
panels.caption: Current models still differ from people across these domains, so better agent design and evaluation are needed.

steps.text: Collect large open-ended traces from domains such as shopping, question answering, and mobility.
Run language-model agents in the same kinds of tasks so that direct comparison is possible.
Score rationality, consistency, and diversity because human-likeness depends on all three.
Check how closely the agent population matches the human population rather than judging only isolated samples.
Identify where models still differ so that future work can target the missing behaviors.

paras: The paper changes evaluation from a few hand-built tests into a population-level comparison between model and human behavior.

hidden.name: Gap between model behavior patterns and human behavior patterns
paras: The key hidden quantity is how far the overall pattern of model behavior is from the overall pattern of human behavior. A single realistic answer does not guarantee that the broader behavior pattern is realistic.

The framework estimates this distance by checking multiple principles. Rationality asks whether actions fit the situation. Consistency asks whether choices remain coherent over time. Diversity asks whether the model population covers enough of the variation seen in people.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark components that strongly influence whether a simulated behavior population resembles a human one.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how close the model's full pattern of behavior is to the human pattern.
Human-likeness is treated as a population-level property measured through rationality, consistency, and diversity across open-ended tasks.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: population-level comparison reveals failures that sample-level tests miss
paras: A few example interactions can make a model look convincing even when its wider behavior population is narrow, repetitive, or inconsistent. Population-level comparison is stronger because it asks whether the model reproduces the broad structure of human behavior across many cases.

Using several principles is also important. An agent can look rational in isolated steps but still fail because its decisions drift over time or because every agent instance behaves too similarly. The framework separates these issues so that evaluation is more diagnostic.

math.h2: Combine several behavior principles into one evaluation view
math.words: A compact view is to give higher human-likeness to a model when its behavior distribution stays close to the human distribution on rationality, consistency, and diversity, while subtracting a penalty for mismatches.
symbols: overall evaluation of how human-like the model behavior is
how often the model's actions make sense for the situation compared with people
how well the model preserves coherent choices over time compared with people
how much of the human variation the model population covers
remaining mismatch between the model behavior distribution and the human distribution

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a shopping agent chooses sensible products in most cases, so rationality match is high.
But it repeats nearly the same preference pattern for every user, so diversity match is low.
It also contradicts its earlier choices in some long sessions, so consistency match is only moderate.
The overall score remains limited because looking plausible in one dimension is not enough.

math.note: The paper uses generic metrics under three principles rather than this exact single formula, but the formula captures how the framework combines those principles.

charts.title: Current strong model
charts.note: The framework finds that even strong models still differ from humans because population diversity and long-run coherence remain limited.

charts.title: Real human behavior target
charts.note: Humans define the target pattern. The gap between these behavior patterns motivates better model design and evaluation because it shows where current systems still differ from people.

items.b: Human data can be biased or incomplete.
items.html: If the collected behavior data reflects only part of the population, the framework may judge models against a narrow target rather than against people more broadly.

items.b: Good aggregate matching can hide bad individual cases.
items.html: A model could match the overall behavior pattern while still behaving poorly for some subgroups, so population-level scores should be paired with subgroup checks.
Performance in shopping, question answering, or mobility may not predict performance in other human activities because each domain has its own behavior structure.
The paper is useful because it turns human-likeness into a scalable computational evaluation problem rather than a handful of ad hoc tests.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small evaluation setup with one open-ended domain, such as shopping. Gather a human behavior set from recorded sessions, then run several agent systems under the same task prompts. Measure situation fit, choice coherence across time, and population spread across many runs.

The demo should show that two agents with similar sample-level quality can differ sharply in population-level human-likeness because one may repeat narrow patterns while the other covers a broader range of coherent behavior.
demo.closing: The demo must prove that human-likeness should be evaluated on broad behavior patterns, not only on a few handpicked examples.
